meta.connection_mode: sqlite3.connect(f'file:{path}?mode=ro', uri=True, timeout=10) — read-only, zero writes
safety_notes: A PRAGMA integrity_check(1) was already running in the background against this same file for 10+ minutes at the start of this investigation (from an earlier session) and was still running throughout — confirms the file is under heavy, slow full-scan-class contention.

A `dbstat` query (SELECT name, SUM(pgsize) FROM dbstat WHERE name LIKE 'transfer_index%' GROUP BY name) was attempted for exact table/index byte sizing. It did not return within a 90s+ budget and was killed (process terminated, exit 144). Table/index byte sizes are therefore NOT_MEASURED exactly; a rough proportional estimate is given instead and clearly labeled.

amount_lamports has no leading-column index (only composite idx_transfer_source_amount_time keyed on source first); EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN confirmed an unfiltered amount_lamports query would be a full covering-index SCAN across ~5.2M rows, so item 6 was answered via bounded id-based sampling instead of an exact count.
No writes, deletes, or schema changes were made. No network/RPC calls were made.

row_count.method: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transfer_index — ran directly, completed in 4.9s (fast; COUNT(*) with no WHERE still benefits from being a simple rowid/index-count style scan on SQLite and was not a problem here).

block_time_range.note_on_min: The min value 1234567890 is a suspicious round decimal-looking Unix timestamp (2009-02-13), far predating Solana/Pump.fun activity — almost certainly a placeholder/sentinel value from a test or default row, not a real on-chain event time. Verified only 2 rows in the entire table have block_time < 1600000000 (2020-09-13), so this does not distort the real distribution.
block_time_range.method: SELECT MIN(block_time), MAX(block_time) FROM transfer_index — used idx_transfer_block_time, completed in 6.5s.

sentinel_low_blocktime_rows.method: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transfer_index WHERE block_time < 1600000000 — indexed range scan, 0.02s.

table_and_index_bytes.attempted_method: SELECT name, SUM(pgsize) FROM dbstat WHERE name LIKE 'transfer_index%' GROUP BY name
table_and_index_bytes.why_abandoned: Did not complete within ~90-120s and was killed; dbstat effectively requires walking the whole btree structure for the table and all 7 indexes on a 13.75GB file with an already-running competing full-scan (integrity_check) and live WAL writers, so it was unsafe to let it run further.

fallback_estimate.method: Proportional estimate from total DB file size and row count, NOT from actual page attribution. total DB file = 14,763,945,984 bytes (page_count 3,605,623 x page_size 4096). transfer_index has ~5.22M rows across 1 table + 7 indexes including 2 partial indexes (idx_transfer_valid, idx_transfer_source_dest) and 1 generated/stored column (amount_sol). transfer_index is known from prior census work to be one of the largest tables in this DB but exact share was not re-verified this run.
fallback_estimate.rough_row_width_estimate_bytes: ~120-180 bytes/row for the base table (id INT + 2x ~44-char base58 addresses + signature ~88 chars + several ints/reals + generated column), which alone would put base table data around 620MB-940MB, plus roughly comparable or greater space in the 7 secondary indexes (composite indexes on 44-char text columns are not cheap) — a plausible total table+indexes footprint in the 1.5-3GB range, but this is an ANALYTICAL GUESS, not a measurement, and should not be treated as authoritative.
fallback_estimate.confidence: LOW — directional only, use for rough sizing conversations, re-run dbstat in a maintenance window with no competing load if an exact figure is needed.

2_ingest_rate.method: Bounded per-day COUNT(*) using WHERE block_time > lo AND block_time <= hi (14 days) and separately WHERE indexed_at > lo AND indexed_at <= hi (7 days), both hitting idx_transfer_block_time / idx_transfer_indexed_at respectively. All per-day queries completed in well under 1s each.

by_block_time_last_14_days.note: block_time is the ON-CHAIN event time, not necessarily the write time — real-world transfer activity clusters, so day-to-day counts vary a lot (77k-402k/day observed).

by_indexed_at_last_7_days.note: indexed_at is the actual write time (unix epoch seconds, REAL). This is a cleaner ingest-rate signal since block_time can be back-filled/delayed relative to write time.

estimated_bytes_per_day.value: NOT_MEASURED_QUERY_TOO_EXPENSIVE for exact bytes; using the same rough per-row estimate as section 1 (~120-180 bytes/row base table, more with indexes), ~200,000 rows/day implies roughly 24-36MB/day of base table data alone, likely 50-100MB/day including index growth. LOW confidence, analytical only.

2_ingest_rate.confidence_overall: HIGH for the row counts themselves (exact, indexed, bounded queries) — MEDIUM for treating ~170k-200k rows/day as a stable steady-state rate, since the 14-day window shows real day-to-day variance (77k to 402k) likely tied to on-chain activity bursts, not a steady linear ingest.

3_consumer_trace.estimation_method: Categorization was done from path conventions, mention density, and light targeted greps (not a full read of every file's logic) — treat category labels as a strong hint for follow-up, not a certified classification. main.py's live-UI classification was verified directly (Flask app + specific 'transfer_index page' route/query code seen).
key_takeaways_for_hot_query_design: src/core/transfer_indexer.py is almost certainly the writer; src/ops/unified_transfer_reader.py is likely the shared read path other modules use — these two plus src/core/main.py (live UI) are the highest-priority files to read in full before finalizing a HOT/COLD boundary design.
src/ops/transfer_cold_store.py already exists and should be read next — there may be partial or prior cold-storage work to build on rather than design from scratch.

Most other consumers (dev_intelligence_*, wallet_clustering, launch_wave_detection, watchtower_detector, etc.) are operation-discovery/classification pipelines, not live low-latency UI paths — they can likely tolerate a HOT+recent-COLD query pattern rather than requiring the full 5.2M rows to stay in a single fast table.

4_operational_significance_classificatio.method_overview: Marker sets were loaded into Python memory (small enough: 21,533 creator_funders.creator_address + 387,114 token_analysis.pf_ws_creator distinct addresses = 395,481 union; 70 wt_ops_v2 operator_entities.entity_address; 7,412 distinct local_operation_discovery_corpus.db direct_funding_edges.funding_signature). A stratified random sample of 20,000 ids was drawn uniformly from id range [1, 6647235] (max observed id; 5,221,462 actual rows exist due to gaps from prior deletes/consolidation) and checked in batched IN(...) lookups (chunks of 1000) against the marker sets for source/destination/signature membership. This keeps every DB query bounded (chunked, id-scoped) while giving statistically representative coverage across the whole table, unlike scanning only recent rows.
4_operational_significance_classificatio.note_on_gaps: 4298 of 20000 sampled ids did not correspond to an existing row — consistent with AUTOINCREMENT id gaps from deletes/updates over the table's life, not a query error.

dimension_a_creator_funding.description: rows where destination OR source is in creator_funders.creator_address UNION token_analysis.pf_ws_creator
dimension_a_creator_funding.estimation_method: SAMPLED (20,000-id stratified sample, 15,702 rows found); extrapolated fraction applied to full table would suggest ~3.66M of 5.22M rows touch a known creator address in some way
dimension_a_creator_funding.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH for the fraction shape, but flagged as surprising and worth validating further: the vast majority of the 0.70 was SOURCE matches (not destination) — i.e., transfers OUTBOUND FROM known creator addresses, not just inbound funding TO creators. This likely reflects creators' ordinary on-chain spend/trading activity being swept into transfer_index broadly, not narrowly 'funding' events. A follow-up should confirm whether unified_transfer_reader.py / main.py's UI actually cares about creator-outbound noise or only creator-inbound funding rows before treating 70% as 'must stay hot'.

dimension_b_operator_entities.description: rows where source OR destination is in wt_ops_v2.db operator_entities.entity_address (70 canonical addresses)
dimension_b_operator_entities.method: EXACT — 70 addresses is small enough for a direct per-address indexed COUNT(*) using idx_transfer_source_time and idx_transfer_destination_time (140 total indexed lookups), no sampling needed.
dimension_b_operator_entities.confidence: HIGH — exact, indexed, ran in 0.11s total
dimension_b_operator_entities.note: This is a tiny fraction (0.006% of all rows) but each hit is a canonical Watchtower/3SW2-confirmed operator address, so per-row significance is very high even though volume is negligible. In the 20,000-row sample used for dimension A, zero operator-entity hits appeared at all (consistent with 292/5.2M being far below sampling resolution at n=20,000) — confirms this dimension needs the exact per-address method, not sampling.

dimension_c_discovery_corpus_signatures.description: rows where signature is in local_operation_discovery_corpus.db direct_funding_edges.funding_signature
dimension_c_discovery_corpus_signatures.method: EXACT — 7,412 distinct signatures checked via chunked IN(...) against transfer_index.signature, which is indexed via the implicit autoindex from the UNIQUE(signature, source, destination) constraint (confirmed via EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: 'SEARCH ... USING COVERING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_transfer_index_1').
dimension_c_discovery_corpus_signatures.note_on_count: 65,099 > 7,412 distinct signatures because a single funding signature/transaction can produce multiple transfer_index rows (e.g. multiple transfers within one tx).

dimension_d_generic_bulk.description: rows with NEITHER endpoint in creator_funders/token_analysis creator sets NOR wt_ops_v2 operator_entities, AND signature NOT in the discovery-corpus funding edges (i.e. fails all three significance tests)
dimension_d_generic_bulk.estimation_method: SAMPLED (same 20,000-id stratified sample used for dimension A, combined with exact-membership checks against all three marker sets loaded in-memory per row)
dimension_d_generic_bulk.confidence: MEDIUM — sampling methodology is sound (uniform stratified over the full id range, three-dimension check applied per sampled row) but the true population fraction could differ by a few points from a single 20k sample; recommend a second independent sample or a full pass if this number drives an irreversible deletion decision.

combined_significance_summary.headline_finding: Roughly 70% of transfer_index rows touch at least one known creator/operator/discovery-corpus reference (dominated overwhelmingly by the creator-address dimension, which itself is dominated by SOURCE=creator matches rather than destination=creator funding events). Only ~30% (an estimated ~1.55M rows) are 'generic bulk' with no known reference on either endpoint and no corpus-linked signature — a materially smaller cold-storage candidate pool than a naive 'most of this table is noise' assumption would suggest.

5_age_vs_significance.population: generic_bulk rows only (the 4,675 sampled rows from item 4 that hit none of the three significance dimensions)
5_age_vs_significance.method: For each generic-bulk row in the same 20,000-id sample, computed age_days = (now - block_time) // 86400 at query time, then bucketed into 30-day windows.
5_age_vs_significance.estimation_method: SAMPLED (n=4675 generic-bulk rows out of the 20,000-id / 15,702-found sample)
interpretation: Generic-bulk rows are heavily front-loaded: 1574/4675 (~33.7%) are within the last 30 days, consistent with the high recent ingest rate observed in item 2 — most bulk rows are recent, not old backlog.

There is a second, smaller cluster around 90-180 days old (528+944+348 ≈ 1820 rows, ~39% of the sample) — this could reflect a burst of past activity or a systematic gap; worth a closer look before picking a HOT window boundary.

The long tail beyond ~270 days thins out substantially but never fully disappears (small counts out to 900+ days), meaning any COLD cutoff will still need to handle a long, low-density tail rather than a hard edge.

A HOT window of roughly 30-60 days would capture the single largest concentration of recent generic-bulk rows; a 90-180 day HOT+WARM tier would additionally capture the second cluster. These are observations to ground a future design discussion, not a recommendation being made here.

6_amount_distribution.description: Fraction of transfer_index rows with amount_lamports < 10,000,000 (0.01 SOL), the dust/low-signal threshold from prior HIGH-confidence discovery calibration work.
6_amount_distribution.why_sampled_not_exact: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN confirmed an unfiltered COUNT(*) WHERE amount_lamports < X would execute as 'SCAN transfer_index USING COVERING INDEX idx_transfer_source_amount_time' — a full index scan across all ~5.2M rows with no source filter to bound it, since amount_lamports is not a leading index column on its own. Given the file's existing contention (concurrent integrity_check + live WAL writers), this was treated as unsafe to run exhaustively and answered via the same bounded id-sample approach instead.
6_amount_distribution.estimation_method: SAMPLED (20,000-id stratified sample, same sample set as item 4/5)
6_amount_distribution.extrapolated_full_table_estimate: ~3.91M of 5.22M rows (0.7491 x 5,221,462 ≈ 3,911,438) are below the 0.01 SOL dust threshold
6_amount_distribution.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH — sample is large (n≈15.7k found rows) and methodology is sound, but this is not an exact count.
6_amount_distribution.cross_reference_note: This 75% dust fraction is notably higher than the 70% 'operationally significant' fraction from item 4, meaning dust and significance are NOT mutually exclusive — many rows touching known creator/operator addresses are still small-amount transfers (consistent with the creator-outbound-spend pattern noted in item 4's dimension A). Amount alone is not a safe proxy for operational insignificance without also checking address/signature membership.
